lines.text: At the crossroads of the Silk Road stand Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva, cities of scholars and conquerors. This is the story of Uzbekistan.
When the ice age ended, the Aral Sea spread between the deserts, once the fourth largest lake on Earth.
By about 700 BCE people were living at Samarkand, one of the oldest cities in Central Asia.
Around it lay Sogdia, whose merchants would carry goods and ideas along the Silk Road all the way to China.
Bukhara grew up as well, a Silk Road city that would one day be a great centre of Islamic learning.
To the west, the walled oasis of Khiva rose from the desert, its inner town still almost whole today.
And by around 200 BCE there was a settlement at Tashkent, now the capital and the largest city in Central Asia.
After Arab armies brought Islam, a scholar from Khwarazm, al-Khwarizmi, gave the world the words algebra and algorithm.
From 819 the Persian Samanids ruled from Bukhara, and the city flourished.
Al-Biruni, born in Khwarazm in 973, would measure the size of the Earth.
Avicenna, born near Bukhara a few years later, would write the Canon of Medicine, taught for centuries in East and West.
After the Mongols laid waste the cities, a new conqueror was born in 1336: Timur, who would build an empire from Samarkand.
From 1370 his empire grew, and Samarkand filled with tiled mosques, tombs and poets.
His grandson Ulugh Beg, born in 1394, would rule as an astronomer king and build a great observatory.
In 1403 work began on the Gur-e-Amir, where Timur himself would be laid to rest.
From 1417 the Registan took shape, the great square of Samarkand, framed by its madrasas.
Babur, a descendant of Timur, would ride south from here and found the Mughal Empire in India.
Back home, from around 1500 the khanates ruled, Bukhara among them, until the Russians came.
Russia took Tashkent in 1865, and Soviet rule followed. In 1938 Islam Karimov was born, the man who would lead the free nation.
Shavkat Mirziyoyev, born in 1957, would succeed him.
In 1966 an earthquake flattened much of Tashkent, and the city was rebuilt in Soviet style.
In 1991, as the Soviet Union fell apart, Uzbekistan became independent, with Karimov as its president.
In 2005, in Andijan, troops fired on protesters and killed hundreds, a dark mark on his long rule.
From Sogdian caravans to an independent nation, Uzbekistan still stands at the heart of the Silk Road.
